title: Emotional awareness
note: These are everyday learning activities about noticing feelings, listening and expressing yourself. They are not therapy, there is no emotional intelligence score, and nothing here diagnoses anything.
support_note: If you are struggling or feel unsafe, please talk to someone you trust or a professional. If you are in danger, contact local emergency services. In the US you can call or text 988; elsewhere, findahelpline.com lists free support.

modules.title: Noticing and naming feelings
modules.summary: Build the habit of noticing what you feel and putting words to it.

lessons.title: Feelings carry information
lessons.text: Feelings often point to something that matters to you: a need, a value or a worry. Noticing them early gives you more choice about what to do next.

lessons.title: More precise words help
lessons.text: "Fine" and "stressed" cover a lot. Words like disappointed, uneasy, relieved or proud can make it easier to understand a feeling and explain it to others.

activities.title: Three check-ins a day
steps: Pick three moments in your day, such as after waking, lunch and the evening.
Each time, name one feeling in one word and where you notice it in your body.
After a week, look for patterns.

activities.title: Swap a vague word
steps: The next time you say "fine" or "stressed", pause.
Find a more precise word for what you feel.
Notice whether the new word changes what you want to do.

modules.reflection: Which feeling do you find hardest to notice or name?

modules.title: Pausing before responding
modules.summary: Create a little space between a feeling and what you say or do.

lessons.title: The useful pause
lessons.text: Strong feelings can make us reply faster than we think. A short pause, even one breath, can be enough to choose a response rather than react.

lessons.title: Reply to the question that matters
lessons.text: Before replying in a tense moment, ask yourself what you want the other person to understand. That question often changes the words you choose.

activities.title: One breath before replying
steps: Choose one conversation today where you will take one slow breath before replying.
Afterwards, note whether your reply was different from your first impulse.
Repeat for a week.

activities.title: Draft, then wait
steps: When a message annoys you, write a reply but don't send it.
Wait at least 20 minutes.
Reread it and ask what you want the other person to understand. Edit before sending.

modules.reflection: When did a quick reply cost you something, and what would a pause have changed?

modules.title: Listening to understand
modules.summary: Listen to understand the other person, not just to reply.

lessons.title: Listening is visible
lessons.text: People feel heard when you show it: summarising what they said, asking a follow-up question, and not rushing to solutions.

lessons.title: Check before you fix
lessons.text: Many people want to be understood before they want advice. Asking "Do you want ideas, or just to talk it through?" avoids a common misunderstanding.

activities.title: Summarise before you respond
steps: In your next important conversation, summarise what you heard before giving your view.
Ask whether you got it right.
Notice how the conversation changes.

activities.title: Ask: ideas or an ear?
steps: When someone tells you about a problem, ask whether they want ideas or someone to listen.
Do what they ask for.
Afterwards, ask whether it helped.

modules.reflection: Who in your life would say you listen well, and what do you do differently with them?

modules.title: Seeing another point of view
modules.summary: Practise imagining how a situation looks and feels to someone else.

lessons.title: Curiosity before conclusions
lessons.text: When someone behaves in a way we don't understand, we often fill the gap with the least generous explanation. Asking what else might be going on keeps curiosity open.

lessons.title: Understanding is not agreeing
lessons.text: You can understand why someone feels the way they do without agreeing with them. Saying so can lower tension in a disagreement.

activities.title: Three explanations
steps: Think of something someone did recently that frustrated you.
Write three different, reasonable explanations for it.
Notice whether your feeling about it changes.

activities.title: Say it in their words
steps: In a disagreement, describe the other person's view so well that they would agree with your summary.
Only then share your own view.
Notice how they respond.

modules.reflection: Whose point of view do you find hardest to imagine, and what would help you understand it?

modules.title: Reflecting on everyday stress
modules.summary: Notice what drains and restores you, and plan small changes.

lessons.title: Stress has patterns
lessons.text: Everyday stress often follows patterns: certain tasks, times of day or situations. Noticing them is the first step to changing what you can.

lessons.title: Recovery matters too
lessons.text: Rest, movement, time outdoors and time with people you like all help many people recover. Small, regular breaks often help more than rare big ones.

activities.title: Drains and restores list
steps: Draw two columns: things that drain you and things that restore you.
Add to them for a week.
Pick one small change: less of one drain, or more of one restorer.

activities.title: Plan micro-breaks
steps: Schedule three five-minute breaks in a busy day.
Use each one for something restoring, such as a short walk or a stretch.
Note how your energy compares with a day without breaks.

modules.reflection: What is one source of everyday stress you could change, and one you need to accept for now?

modules.title: Understanding others' needs
modules.summary: Notice what others might need from a conversation, and ask rather than assume.

lessons.title: Different people, different needs
lessons.text: In the same situation, one person may want reassurance, another a plan, another some space. Noticing the difference helps you respond in a way that fits.

lessons.title: Ask, don't guess
lessons.text: Signals like tone or silence can be read many ways. A simple question such as "How are you finding this?" is more reliable than guessing.

activities.title: A quick needs check
steps: Before a meeting or conversation, think about what each person might need from it.
During it, ask one person directly how they are finding it.
Afterwards, compare what you guessed with what you learned.

activities.title: Notice the quiet one
steps: In a group conversation, notice who has said the least.
Invite their view without putting them on the spot, for example after the meeting.
Note what you learned.

modules.reflection: Whose needs do you tend to overlook, and how could you check in with them?

modules.title: Expressing feelings constructively
modules.summary: Say how you feel and what you need in a way others can hear.

lessons.title: Describe, don't blame
lessons.text: "When the plan changed at the last minute, I felt frustrated because I had prepared" is easier to hear than "You always change things". Describe the situation, your feeling and why.

lessons.title: Make a clear request
lessons.text: Feelings are easier to act on when they come with a specific, doable request, such as "Could we agree changes a day in advance?"

activities.title: Situation, feeling, request
steps: Think of something that bothered you recently.
Write it as: when (situation), I felt (feeling) because (reason). Could we (request)?
If it feels right, use it in a real conversation.

activities.title: Say the good feelings too
steps: Each day this week, tell someone one specific thing they did that you appreciated.
Say how it made you feel.
Notice how people respond.

modules.reflection: Which feeling do you tend to keep to yourself, and what might change if you shared it?
